processing: Ordinary steamed sencha blended with preserved cherry leaves and blossom petals; some versions use salted or sugared leaf, and some add a little matcha.
harvest_season: The base sencha follows the usual Japanese spring picking; the blend itself is most often associated with the cherry blossom season.
appearance_dry: Dark green sencha needles mixed with brownish cherry leaf pieces and pale pink petals.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green, typical of sencha, sometimes slightly cloudier when matcha is included.
appearance_wet: Soft green sencha leaf with darker softened pieces of cherry leaf and opened petals.
taste_profile: Grassy, gently brisk sencha under a floral sweetness that many drinkers compare to sakura mochi; preserved leaf can add a light salty edge.

brewing.notes: Treat it like a sencha, not a herbal tea: around 80°C and a couple of minutes. Hotter water pushes bitterness over the delicate blossom note.

vintage_note: Sold as a non-vintage flavoured blend, usually without a harvest year on the pack and often promoted in spring. As with other Japanese green teas it is best drunk fresh, within about a year of packing, since the aroma of both sencha and blossom fades.
description:
Sakura sencha is not a single regional tea but a style of blend: Japanese sencha combined with cherry leaves, petals or both. Producers in Shizuoka and Shimane are among those who sell it, and recipes differ from one maker to the next.

The tea base is made as normal sencha. The character comes from the cherry material, which may be preserved with salt or sugar, and that choice shows in the cup: some versions lean sweet, others have a faint saltiness. A few add matcha for colour and body.

Expect familiar green sencha flavour with a floral, almost confectionery sweetness on top; the comparison drinkers reach for is sakura mochi. Keep the water near 80°C and do not stretch the steep, or the sencha turns bitter and covers the flower.

Read the ingredient list before buying. Blends with real leaf and petals are different from teas with added flavouring, and there is no protected standard for the name. Shizu-7132 is worth trying next: a pure sencha cultivar with a natural cherry-leaf scent and nothing blended in.
history: Little is documented about when or by whom this blend was first made. It is a modern commercial style rather than a historic named tea, built on the familiar Japanese use of preserved cherry leaves and blossoms in food and drink.
